name: The Mere-Exposure Effect
statement: The more often we encounter something, the more we tend to like it.
statementAccent: the more we tend to like it
meaning: People develop a preference for things simply because they are familiar with them. Repeated exposure to a face, a tune, a word, a shape, or a logo increases liking for it, independent of any reward, argument, or new information. Familiarity alone nudges attitude in a positive direction.
mechanism: The leading account is processing fluency: repeated exposure makes a stimulus easier to perceive and process, and that ease is experienced as, or misattributed to, positive feeling. Zajonc framed it in evolutionary terms — a novel stimulus first triggers wariness, which fades with repeated harmless exposure, leaving interest and liking. Strikingly, the effect occurs even without conscious recognition: stimuli flashed too briefly to be consciously perceived still shift liking, which led Zajonc to argue that preferences can precede and bypass cognition.

examples.text: Zajonc showed people nonsense words and unfamiliar characters varying numbers of times, and the more frequently seen ones were rated more positively — the founding demonstration.

People tend to prefer the mirror-reversed image of their own face, the view they see daily, while their friends prefer the true image, the view others habitually see — each preferring the more familiar version.
Stimuli presented too briefly for conscious recognition still produce a reliable liking bias toward the repeated items, showing the effect works without any felt sense of familiarity.

variants.name: Processing fluency
variants.text: The leading mechanistic account, in which the ease of processing a familiar stimulus is misread as liking for it.

variants.name: The propinquity effect
variants.text: The interpersonal cousin, in which physical or psychological proximity and frequent contact increase attraction and liking between people.

whyItMatters: It is a robust, quantitatively supported explanation for why familiarity breeds liking — central to advertising, branding, propaganda, aesthetics, and interpersonal attraction. That it can operate without conscious recognition makes it theoretically important, suggesting affect can arise ahead of thought.

working.text: expect familiarity from repeated exposure to raise liking, which is why advertisers and campaigners repeat their messages.
notice when you like something merely because it is familiar rather than for its merits.
stop short of saturation, since liking peaks and then declines as repetition breeds boredom.

limits: The effect is well replicated — a meta-analysis pooling roughly two hundred studies found it reliable — but it is not monotonic. Liking rises with early exposures, peaks, and then declines with excessive repetition as boredom and satiation set in, an inverted-U rather than an endless climb. It is strongest for novel stimuli and for brief or subliminal exposures, and a delay before rating tends to strengthen it, while it is weaker for children and for complex visual art. So more exposure helps only up to a point.
misreadings: It does not mean more exposure always increases liking — beyond a peak, repetition breeds boredom and liking falls. And it is not driven by a conscious sense of familiarity; it works even when people cannot recognise having seen the stimulus.
origin: Established by Robert Zajonc in 'Attitudinal Effects of Mere Exposure,' Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 9(2, Part 2):1-27 (1968), a monograph supplement.

sources.text: Zajonc, R. (1968). “Attitudinal effects of mere exposure.” Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, vol. 9. — the monograph reporting the original experiments.
